Everything else is free or open source. And one file in there was never supposed to ship at all.
PengPong is a survivors-like where a penguin with a hockey stick whacks whatever is in front of it. Guns. Pufferfish. Other penguins.
It's from a Korean studio called SANDY FLOOR, and the full game came out on August twentieth.
The demo sits at eighty six percent, the full game at eighty five. Nearly all of the praise is for the art.
Nineteen thirties rubber-hose cartoon. Cuphead comes up in review after review. That look normally costs a lot of money.
So that was my question. What did this team buy, and what did they build.
Steam publishes the list of files a demo installs. PengPong's is two hundred and eighty two files, two point six eight gigabytes.
The first clue is a folder name. MonoBleedingEdge.
Unity builds your code one of two ways. IL2CPP turns the C# into native code and fuses it into one block. Mono leaves the DLLs as they are.
PengPong is Mono. So everything this team pulled in is sitting there under its own file name.
Audio is FMOD. Four sound bank files, twenty nine megabytes.
Take this one with you. FMOD is free below two hundred thousand dollars a year in revenue. There is no reason an indie can't use commercial audio middleware.
The paid items are exactly two. Text Animator, sixty five dollars. Ara Trails, thirty.
DOTween, GameAnalytics, UIParticle, NavMeshPlus. All free, or open source.
So what did they animate that Cuphead look with. Normally that's Spine, and a personal licence for Spine is three hundred and forty nine dollars.
There is no Spine in this build. There is Unity's own 2D Animation package, and the IK package next to it.
Same idea. You put bones in a drawing and move the bones. And you get it from the Package Manager for nothing.
Now the strangest thing in the list. Assembly-CSharp.dll is five kilobytes.
Unless you tell it otherwise, Unity puts all of your game code in that one file. Five kilobytes means the code has been moved out.
The mechanism is called an Assembly Definition, asmdef for short. One small file in a folder, and that folder compiles to its own DLL.
What you get is compile time. Change one line and only that module rebuilds, not the whole project. The bigger the project, the bigger the difference.
Eight modules came out of this, and every one carries the studio's name. SandyToolkit. SandyAudio. SandyPooling. SandySetting. SandyDependency.
Pooling, audio, settings, dependency injection. The things you rewrite for every game. This team carries them to the next project as folders.
Saves go through SQLite. With over three hundred items, that beats one big JSON file.
Content is split into seventeen Addressables bundles, five hundred and twenty nine megabytes. A patch only downloads the bundles that changed.
There's a Localization package too. Eight languages go through it.
And then two things that should not be in a release build. The first is Unity Recorder, an editor tool for capturing video. Harmless. Somebody forgot to take it out.
The second is MCP for Unity. That's the open source bridge that lets an AI model drive the Unity editor directly.
What I can confirm is that the file is in the shipped build. How much they used it, and for what, only the developer knows.
My guess is it was wired up for development and went out with everything else. If I'm wrong, say so in the comments and I'll pin the correction.
For scale: of the two point six eight gigabytes, art and sound are two point two. All one hundred and ninety five DLLs together are ninety one megabytes.
Now the reviews of the full game, where the complaints land in one place. It launched with three stages.
Tools outlive the game they were built for. But the hours that went into them are hours this game's content did not get.
Eight frameworks and three stages. Those two numbers come from the same team.
Here's the whole teardown on one card.
Unity, Mono. Ninety five dollars of paid assets. Unity 2D Animation instead of Spine. Eight in-house modules. Three stages.
Worth a dip. The demo is free, and hitting things with that stick feels as good as it looks.
Three things to take away. FMOD is free for indies. You can do bone animation without paying for Spine. And splitting your code into asmdefs is what makes a big project compile fast.
